stage-0.q: Why is recognizing whether an image contains a cat a task for machine learning rather than a hand-coded rules program?
options: A rules program would require thousands of if-statements for lighting, angles, fur, and poses that no human can completely specify
Computers are unable to execute if-statements on pixel values
Machine learning models run faster than hand-written rules on simple tasks
Rules programs can only work with numbers, while images are made of colors
stage-0.why: Nobody can write down rules covering every variation in lighting, angle, and pose for a cat. Machine learning turns examples into patterns instead of requiring manual rules.

stage-0.q: In machine learning, what do we mean when we call a model 'a function with knobs'?
options: The learner manually turns physical dials on their computer keyboard to control accuracy
The model has internal parameters that adjust its behavior; training means automatically adjusting those knobs until predictions match reality
The model only works if the programmer defines preset slider controls in a web browser
The knobs represent the speed of the processor during calculations
stage-0.why: A model has parameters (the knobs). Training is the automatic process where an algorithm turns those knobs to minimize the difference between predictions and actual labels.

stage-0.q: Suppose you want to compute the total error across 500 house price predictions. In Python, what pattern best describes this?
options: Store the prices in a list, iterate through them with a for-loop, and accumulate the difference between prediction and actual price into a running sum
Write 500 separate variable names like error1, error2, ..., error500 and manually add them
Define an if-statement that checks whether house prices are positive
Create a single number variable and overwrite it 500 times without adding
stage-0.why: Lists hold sequential data, loops repeat actions across each item, and accumulator variables gather the total error across all examples.

stage-0.q: Why do programmers write reusable functions (using 'def') when scoring models instead of copying and pasting the error calculation?
options: Python refuses to execute code blocks that appear more than once in a file
Functions give a name to an idea, prevent copy-paste bugs, and let you calculate error on new datasets with a single call
Functions automatically turn non-linear models into linear equations
Copying code makes the Python interpreter run out of RAM
stage-0.why: Packaging logic inside a function creates a reliable, reusable tool that tests any prediction against true values without duplicate code.

stage-0.q: In mathematical formulas for machine learning, what does the Greek uppercase letter Sigma (Σ) tell you to do?
options: Add up a sequence of numbers or errors across all items in a group
Multiply two matrices together
Take the square root of the largest error
Check whether a number is greater than zero
stage-0.why: Uppercase Sigma (Σ) stands for sum: it simply means 'add all of these terms together', exactly like a loop accumulating a total in code.

stage-0.q: When looking at the graph of a line predicting trip duration from miles driven, what does the slope tell you?
options: The baseline trip duration when the car drives zero miles
How many additional minutes the trip takes for each additional mile driven
The total number of trips in the dataset
The exact error made on the longest trip
stage-0.why: Slope measures rate of change: for every 1 unit increase in the input (miles), the output (minutes) increases by the slope.

stage-0.q: Before a machine learning model deployed on the web can classify an uploaded photo, why must preprocessing occur first?
options: The web browser cannot upload binary files
The model was trained on pictures of a specific size, crop, and color scale, so user uploads must be converted into the exact numerical format the model expects
Preprocessing increases the file size so the server doesn't reject it as spam
Uploading raw photos is forbidden by internet protocols
stage-0.why: Models expect fixed numerical inputs (e.g., 224x224 pixels, normalized values). If you pass an arbitrary raw image without preprocessing, the model cannot read it.

stage-0.q: What is the difference between training a model and deploying a model?
options: Training fits the knobs using historical data; deploying puts the frozen model where users or systems can send new inputs and get live predictions
Training runs on a phone while deploying runs in a cloud cluster
Training converts code into math while deploying converts math into text
Deploying is only needed for unsupervised models, while supervised models run directly from training
stage-0.why: Training finds the best parameters using examples and loss. Deployment packages the resulting model as an API or application for live real-world use.

stage-1.q: Geometrically, what does a 2x2 matrix with a determinant of zero do to the 2D plane?
options: It collapses the entire 2D plane onto a 1D line or a single 0D point, losing information so it cannot be undone
It rotates the plane by 90 degrees without changing areas
It doubles the area of any shape on the plane
It reflects the plane across the diagonal axis
stage-1.why: The determinant measures how much area is scaled by the transformation. A determinant of 0 collapses 2D area into zero (a line or point), which has no inverse.

stage-1.q: Why can an overdetermined system of linear equations (more rows than columns, representing more equations than variables) rarely be solved exactly?
options: The target vector usually lies outside the column space spanned by the matrix columns
Matrices with more rows than columns cannot be multiplied by vectors
Elimination cannot be performed if the number of rows exceeds two
Overdetermined matrices always have negative eigenvalues
stage-1.why: The columns span a subspace. If the target y doesn't sit exactly inside that subspace, no linear combination of columns equals y, requiring least squares approximation.

stage-1.q: When optimizing a cost function with gradient descent, why do we update parameters in the direction of the negative gradient (-∇L)?
options: The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent, so the negative gradient points in the direction of steepest local descent
The negative gradient points directly at the global minimum regardless of function shape
Negative gradients prevent parameters from becoming positive
Multiplying by -1 ensures the learning rate stays between 0 and 1
stage-1.why: The gradient ∇L points uphill toward steepest increase; stepping in the opposite direction (-∇L) guarantees the fastest instantaneous decrease in loss.

stage-1.q: If y = f(u) and u = g(x), why is the derivative dy/dx equal to (dy/du) * (du/dx) rather than (dy/du) + (du/dx)?
options: Derivatives represent multiplicative rates of change (stretching factors); chained rates of change compound by multiplying
Addition is not defined for differential equations in calculus
Multiplication guarantees the derivative will always be positive
The plus sign is reserved for vector additions only
stage-1.why: Derivatives are ratios of change (slopes). If y moves 3x faster than u, and u moves 2x faster than x, y moves (3 * 2) = 6x faster than x.

stage-1.q: Suppose z = f(x, y). What does the Jacobian matrix or gradient vector collect for functions with multiple inputs and outputs?
options: All the first-order partial derivatives showing how each output changes with respect to each input
The second derivatives indicating the curvature in all directions
The determinant of the input vectors
The eigenvalues of the input covariance matrix
stage-1.why: The Jacobian matrix packs all partial derivatives ∂y_i / ∂x_j, describing the best local linear approximation of a multi-variable function.

stage-1.q: A medical test is 99% accurate (1% false positive, 1% false negative). If a condition affects 1 in 10,000 people, why is a person testing positive still unlikely to have the condition?
options: The prior base rate (1 in 10,000) is so low that false positives among healthy people vastly outnumber true positives from infected people
Medical tests become ineffective when given to large populations
Bayes theorem cannot be applied when probabilities are under 50%
The false negative rate cancels out the true positive rate
stage-1.why: Out of 10,000 people, 1 has the disease (detected ~1), but ~100 healthy people test false positive (1% of 9,999). So P(disease | positive) is ~1/101 (~1%).

stage-1.q: Why is the median often preferred over the mean when describing subway delays, income, or web request latencies?
options: The mean is sensitive to extreme outliers and long right tails, whereas the median reflects the experience of the typical observation
The median is always a larger number than the mean
The median can only be computed when data follows a Gaussian normal distribution
Computing the mean requires sorting all numbers, which is computationally expensive
stage-1.why: Extreme values (like a 2-hour subway signal failure) pull the mean far to the right, while the median remains robust to outliers.

stage-1.q: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), what do the top eigenvectors or principal singular vectors represent?
options: The orthogonal directions in feature space along which the data exhibits the maximum variance
The labels with the lowest classification error
The features that have zero correlation with any other variable
The points that lie closest to the origin
stage-1.why: The first principal component is the direction of greatest variance in the data; subsequent components capture orthogonal directions of remaining variance.

stage-2.q: What happens if a neural network with 10 hidden layers uses purely linear activation functions (no non-linearities like ReLU or sigmoid)?
options: The entire network collapses mathematically into a single linear transformation (matrix multiplication), unable to learn non-linear boundaries
The network fits any arbitrary continuous function due to the universal approximation theorem
The gradients explode to infinity on the very first backpropagation step
The network can only output values between 0 and 1
stage-2.why: A product of linear transformations W_2 * (W_1 * x) is just a single linear transformation W_combined * x. Non-linearities are required to learn non-linear patterns.

stage-2.q: Why does reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation) scale much better for neural network training than forward-mode differentiation?
options: Neural networks typically have millions of parameters but only one scalar loss; reverse mode computes all parameter gradients in one backward pass
Forward-mode requires computing matrix determinants while reverse mode only uses vector sums
Reverse-mode prevents gradient saturation in sigmoid neurons
Forward-mode only works for convex optimization problems
stage-2.why: Reverse mode takes O(outputs) backward passes. Since training minimizes a single scalar loss (1 output) across millions of weights, reverse mode computes all gradients in a single sweep.

stage-2.q: Why does high second-order curvature (large eigenvalues in the Hessian matrix) cause gradient descent with a constant learning rate to diverge or oscillate?
options: Steep valley walls cause the gradient to change direction drastically after a small step, overshooting the minimum back and forth
Second-order curvature sets the first derivatives to zero immediately
High curvature guarantees that the loss function has no stationary points
The Hessian matrix can only be inverted when all gradients are zero
stage-2.why: When curvature is high (the function bends sharply), a first-order linear step based on local slope shoots past the turn, causing wild oscillations or divergence.

stage-2.q: Why is minimizing cross-entropy loss equivalent to Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) for classification models?
options: Minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the true classes is mathematically identical to minimizing cross-entropy between true and predicted distributions
Cross-entropy loss forces the model weights to sum to 1
MLE only works when the loss function is mean squared error
Cross-entropy replaces gradient descent with an analytical matrix inversion
stage-2.why: The likelihood of independent samples is ∏ P(y_i|x_i). Taking the negative logarithm gives -∑ log P(y_i|x_i), which is exactly the multiclass cross-entropy loss.

stage-2.q: What does the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence D_KL(P || Q) measure between a true distribution P and a predicted distribution Q?
options: The extra information (bits or nats) required to encode samples from P when using the code optimized for Q
The symmetric Euclidean distance between the mean vectors of P and Q
The probability that a sample drawn from P is identical to a sample from Q
The correlation coefficient between the random variables
stage-2.why: KL divergence measures the relative entropy or information lost when approximating distribution P with distribution Q. It is zero if and only if P == Q.

stage-2.q: How does L2 weight decay (adding λ * ||w||² to the loss) connect to Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation?
options: It is mathematically equivalent to placing a zero-mean Gaussian prior distribution on the network weights
It forces all weights to be exactly zero for feature selection
It assumes weights follow a Laplace distribution with heavy tails
It turns non-convex neural network losses into globally convex quadratics
stage-2.why: In Bayesian MAP, log P(w|D) = log P(D|w) + log P(w). If the prior P(w) is Gaussian N(0, σ²), log P(w) contributes -||w||²/(2σ²), which is L2 weight decay.

stage-2.q: Why do deep networks using sigmoid or tanh activations suffer from vanishing gradients when networks using ReLU do not?
options: The derivative of sigmoid saturates near 0 when inputs are large positive or negative, causing gradients to shrink exponentially as they multiply backward
Sigmoid activations cause weights to become negative during initialization
ReLU functions have a derivative of zero for all inputs, preventing gradients from multiplying
Sigmoid layers can only be trained with second-order Newton-Raphson methods
stage-2.why: Sigmoid's maximum derivative is 0.25. Chaining several layers multiplies numbers <= 0.25, driving gradients to near zero. ReLU has derivative 1 for positive inputs, passing gradients undiminished.

stage-2.q: In PyTorch, why must you call 'optimizer.zero_grad()' before running 'loss.backward()' in each training step?
options: PyTorch accumulates gradients into .grad buffers by default; without resetting, gradients from previous batches add together
zero_grad() resets the model weights to random initial values
Calling backward() without zero_grad() raises a CUDA Out of Memory exception
zero_grad() normalizes the learning rate to prevent exploding loss
stage-2.why: PyTorch sums gradients on each backward() call (useful for RNNs or gradient accumulation). If you forget zero_grad(), you optimize against the sum of all past batches.

stage-3.q: During training, your model's training loss continues to fall toward zero, but validation loss begins rising after epoch 12. What is occurring?
options: The model is overfitting: it is memorizing noise in the training set and losing generalizability to unseen data
The learning rate has automatically decayed to zero
The validation dataset has become corrupted by gradient descent
The model has underfit and needs more training epochs
stage-3.why: When training error decreases while validation error increases, the model's capacity exceeds the general pattern and it begins fitting sample-specific noise (overfitting).

stage-3.q: In a cancer screening system where missing a malignant tumor has disastrous consequences, which metric should be prioritized over overall accuracy?
options: Recall (sensitivity), minimizing false negatives so almost no actual cases are missed
Precision, ensuring that no healthy patients are ever flagged
Specificity alone, without regard to positive detection rates
Inference latency on mobile hardware
stage-3.why: Recall = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives). High recall ensures that very few sick patients slip through undetected.

stage-3.q: Why is performing feature normalization (like subtracting the mean and dividing by standard deviation) on the entire dataset BEFORE splitting into train and test a dangerous mistake?
options: It causes data leakage: information from the test distribution leaks into the training pipeline, yielding overly optimistic evaluation scores
Standardization makes scikit-learn classifiers unable to converge
Test sets cannot contain negative numbers after normalization
It changes the row order of the dataset
stage-3.why: The test set must simulate unseen future data. Computing test statistics into the scaler leaks information about the test distribution into training.

stage-3.q: You evaluate a new model against your production baseline on 200 test examples. Accuracy rises from 82% to 84%, but a statistical test yields p = 0.35. What should you conclude?
options: The 2% gain could easily be random sampling noise; there is not enough evidence to claim model B is truly better
Model B is guaranteed to be 84% accurate on all future traffic
The baseline model is broken and should be retired immediately
A p-value of 0.35 means model B has a 35% chance of overfitting
stage-3.why: A p-value of 0.35 means that if both models were identical, a 2% discrepancy would occur by chance 35% of the time. The difference is not statistically significant.

stage-3.q: What is the primary difference in how Random Forests and Gradient Boosted Trees build their ensembles?
options: Random Forests train deep independent trees in parallel to reduce variance (bagging); Gradient Boosting trains shallow trees sequentially to correct prior errors (boosting)
Random Forests only work for regression while Gradient Boosting only works for classification
Random Forests optimize cross-entropy using backpropagation while Boosting uses neural networks
Random Forests cannot handle numerical features
stage-3.why: Random forest averages uncorrelated deep trees to slash variance. Gradient boosting fits successive trees to the pseudo-residuals of earlier trees to slash bias.

stage-3.q: When predicting whether a bank customer will default next month, including 'total late fees charged in the current month' as a feature creates what problem?
options: Target leakage: the feature records an outcome that only occurs after default has already begun, which won't be available at prediction time
High variance due to numerical underflow
Collinearity with the learning rate schedule
Violation of the Central Limit Theorem
stage-3.why: Target leakage occurs when a feature reflects information that becomes known only at or after the target event occurs, producing fake perfect accuracy that fails in real life.

stage-3.q: If error analysis reveals that your model has high bias (both training error and validation error are unacceptably high), which action is most effective?
options: Increase model capacity (e.g. deeper trees, more parameters, or richer features)
Collect 100,000 more training examples of the same format
Increase L2 regularization penalty by a factor of 10
Apply early stopping at epoch 2
stage-3.why: High bias means the model cannot even fit the training data (underfitting). Collecting more data or adding regularization makes underfitting worse; you need a more expressive model.

stage-3.q: How does an Isolation Forest identify anomalous data points in an unlabelled dataset?
options: Anomalies have unusual feature values, so random recursive partition cuts isolate them in far fewer splits than normal points
It trains a neural network classifier to predict whether a point is prime
It computes the convex hull and flags all interior points as anomalies
It groups all points into a single cluster and measures total variance
stage-3.why: Because anomalies are few and structurally distinct, random partitioning splits isolate them close to the tree roots with very short average path lengths.

stage-4.q: In NumPy, what are the resulting shape and mechanism when adding array A of shape (100, 1) and array B of shape (1, 50)?
options: Shape (100, 50), via broadcasting without copying data in memory
Shape (100, 1), because the first dimension dominates
A ValueError, because dimensions do not match exactly
Shape (101, 51), by concatenating the edges
stage-4.why: NumPy broadcasting compares shapes elementwise from right to left. Dimension 1 stretches to match 50, and dimension 1 stretches to match 100, producing (100, 50) without memory duplication.

stage-4.q: Why does scikit-learn separate '.fit()' and '.transform()' on preprocessing transformers inside a Pipeline?
options: fit() computes parameters (like mean and variance) strictly from the training data, while transform() applies those frozen parameters to new datasets
fit() converts data to Python lists, while transform() converts it back to NumPy
fit() only runs on GPUs, while transform() runs on CPUs
Calling fit() twice in a row causes the pipeline to self-destruct
stage-4.why: This distinction prevents leakage: you learn the scaling parameters strictly on training folds, then apply those exact parameters to validation and test data.

stage-4.q: How does the Adam optimizer improve over standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with a fixed learning rate?
options: It tracks exponentially decaying moving averages of both past gradients (momentum) and squared gradients (adaptive learning rates per parameter)
It computes the exact analytical inverse of the Hessian matrix at every step
It eliminates the need for calculating backpropagation gradients
It guarantees that training loss drops monotonically at every single step
stage-4.why: Adam combines momentum (smoothing noisy gradients) and RMSprop (scaling steps inversely by gradient magnitude variance), allowing fast progress along flat ravines.

stage-4.q: What problem does Batch Normalization primarily solve during the training of deep networks?
options: It standardizes layer activations across mini-batches, stabilizing internal covariate shift and preventing activations from blowing up or vanishing
It compresses model weights onto disk so they take up less storage
It replaces all activation functions with unit-step functions
It prevents GPUs from running out of CUDA registers
stage-4.why: By normalizing activations to zero mean and unit variance per batch (with learnable scale and shift), Batch Norm keeps intermediate layer distributions stable.

stage-4.q: Why is a learning rate warmup (gradually increasing learning rate over the first few hundred steps) frequently used when training large models with large batch sizes?
options: Early in training, random initial weights produce erratic gradients; warmup prevents catastrophic destructive weight updates before statistics stabilize
GPUs require time to physically warm up their memory circuits
Warmup allows the model to calculate the test set accuracy before starting training
Warmup prevents Python from garbage-collecting the optimizer
stage-4.why: With randomly initialized weights, initial gradient estimates are wildly inaccurate. Taking huge initial steps can shatter good representations.

stage-4.q: When profiling GPU training, you observe 30% GPU utilization while CPU usage is pinned at 100%. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: The data loading and preprocessing pipeline on the CPU cannot supply batches fast enough to keep the GPU fed
The GPU does not have enough compute cores to process tensors
The model learning rate is set too low
Gradient descent requires CPU confirmation before each GPU kernel launch
stage-4.why: When the CPU is maxed out and the GPU is idling at low utilization, data ingestion (reading from disk, decoding, augmenting) is starving the GPU of input tensors.

stage-4.q: Why is setting 'torch.manual_seed(42)' and 'np.random.seed(42)' sometimes insufficient by itself to guarantee bit-for-bit reproducibility across GPU runs?
options: Certain GPU CUDA operations (like atomic adds in backward passes) execute non-deterministically across parallel threads unless deterministic flags are explicitly enabled
Random seeds in Python only affect strings, not floating-point numbers
GPUs do not support seed initialization
Network latency on the internet alters matrix multiplications
stage-4.why: Atomic floating point summation across unordered GPU threads yields tiny rounding variations unless `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` is enabled.

stage-4.q: During training of a deep ReLU network, 80% of neurons suddenly stop firing (outputting 0 for all training examples) and their gradients remain 0 forever. What is this phenomenon?
options: Dying ReLU: large negative gradient updates pushed neuron biases so far negative that inputs never exceed zero
Weight decay successfully pruning the entire network
Gradient ascent escaping local minima
Catastrophic forgetting caused by high batch size
stage-4.why: When a ReLU neuron's inputs are always <= 0, its activation is 0 and its derivative is 0. No gradient flows back to update its weights, permanently killing the neuron.

zoo.q: How does the geometry of the decision boundary drawn by a Decision Tree differ fundamentally from that of Logistic Regression?
options: Decision trees create axis-aligned orthogonal step boundaries (rectangles), while logistic regression creates a single continuous linear hyperplane
Decision trees always create concentric circles, while logistic regression creates wavy curves
Logistic regression cannot separate classes if there are more than two features
Decision trees require normalized data between 0 and 1 while logistic regression does not
zoo.why: Each tree split tests a single feature against a threshold (x_i <= c), cutting feature space into axis-aligned rectangular boxes. Logistic regression draws w^T x + b = 0.

zoo.q: Why does Lasso regression (L1 penalty) produce sparse models with exact zero coefficients, while Ridge regression (L2 penalty) only shrinks weights toward zero?
options: The L1 constraint region is a diamond with sharp corners on the coordinate axes, where loss contours frequently touch the axes first
Lasso uses gradient descent while Ridge uses pseudo-inverses
Ridge regression only works when all features are independent
L1 regularization multiplies the loss by zero for unimportant features
zoo.why: The diamond geometry of the L1 ball ||w||_1 <= C has corners resting on the coordinate axes. The optimal elliptical loss contour hits these corners, zeroing out coefficients.

zoo.q: How does the 'kernel trick' in Support Vector Machines (SVM) enable linear algorithms to learn complex non-linear boundaries?
options: It computes inner products in a high-dimensional feature space using a kernel function k(x, x') without explicitly calculating the high-dimensional coordinates
It replaces optimization with a deep convolution network
It converts continuous variables into discrete binary flags
It splits the training set into thousands of micro-batches
zoo.why: Because the dual formulation of SVM depends only on inner products x_i · x_j, replacing the dot product with a kernel function k(x_i, x_j) computes high-dimensional distances implicitly.

zoo.q: Why do gradient boosted decision trees (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) consistently dominate neural networks on tabular datasets?
options: They are invariant to feature scaling, handle missing values naturally, and capture sharp threshold interactions without requiring delicate architectural tuning
Trees run on quantum hardware while neural networks run on CPUs
Tabular data cannot be converted into floating-point numbers for neural networks
Gradient boosted trees have provably zero generalization error on tables
zoo.why: Tabular data consists of heterogeneous, unaligned features and discrete rules. Tree algorithms require no normalization, handle missing data directly, and partition thresholds cleanly.

zoo.q: Why is k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) uniquely fragile when applied to datasets with unnormalized features (e.g., age 0-80 alongside income 0-200,000)?
options: Euclidean distance will be almost entirely dominated by the feature with the largest numerical range (income), rendering age irrelevant
k-NN cannot calculate distances if any feature exceeds 100
Unnormalized features cause the k parameter to become negative
The algorithm requires inverting a singular matrix of feature variances
zoo.why: Euclidean distance sums squared differences. A difference of $1,000 in income dwarfs a difference of 10 years in age unless features are standardized.

zoo.q: What core assumption gives Naive Bayes its name, and why does it often produce poor probability calibration even when classification accuracy is high?
options: It naively assumes all features are conditionally independent given the class; correlated features multiply their evidence, pushing probabilities to extreme 0 or 1
It assumes all data points were generated by a coin toss
It refuses to update its prior beliefs regardless of new evidence
It only works on binary classification tasks
zoo.why: Naive Bayes assumes P(x_1, ..., x_n | y) = ∏ P(x_i | y). Redundant correlated features double-count evidence, ranking items correctly but producing overconfident, uncalibrated probabilities.

zoo.q: Why are individual trees in a Random Forest typically grown deep without pruning, while trees in Gradient Boosting are kept shallow (depth 3-6)?
options: Random Forest averages deep, high-variance trees to slash variance; Boosting sequentially builds weak, low-variance learners to gradually eliminate bias
Deep trees cannot be trained with gradient descent
Boosting crashes if a tree has more than 8 leaves
Random Forest algorithms only work if each tree has 100% training accuracy
zoo.why: Bagging needs low-bias, high-variance individual trees because averaging reduces variance. Boosting needs low-variance weak learners so step-by-step additions don't overfit.

zoo.q: If your production service must classify high-frequency financial transactions within 200 microseconds on a single CPU core, which model family is best suited?
options: Logistic regression or small linear models, which require only a single dot product and scalar sigmoid evaluation
A 50-tree Random Forest with depth 20
A k-nearest neighbor classifier with 500,000 stored points
A deep convolutional neural network
zoo.why: Evaluating w^T x + b is a vector dot product of dozens of numbers, taking nanoseconds in CPU cache. k-NN requires scanning half a million points, and deep forests require dozens of pointer hops.

stage-5.q: What two spatial inductive biases make convolutional layers (CNNs) far more parameter-efficient than fully connected layers for images?
options: Local connectivity (pixels nearby interact most) and weight sharing (features like edges can appear anywhere in the image)
Rotation invariance and scale invariance
Frequency decomposition and continuous Fourier projection
Global attention and autoregressive masking
stage-5.why: A fully connected layer on a 1000x1000 image requires a trillion weights. CNNs share a tiny 3x3 kernel across all spatial locations, drastically cutting parameters.

stage-5.q: Why did modern CNN architectures (like VGG and ResNet) replace large 7x7 convolutional kernels with stacks of two or three 3x3 kernels?
options: Stacking two 3x3 convolutions has the same 5x5 receptive field but uses fewer parameters and introduces multiple non-linear activations
3x3 convolutions run on GPUs while 7x7 convolutions can only run on CPUs
7x7 kernels cannot be trained with backpropagation
Odd-sized kernels greater than 3 cause image boundary reflections
stage-5.why: Two 3x3 kernels use 2 * (3*3) = 18 weights vs 5*5 = 25 weights, while providing two non-linear ReLU stages instead of one, increasing expressive power.

stage-5.q: In modern object detectors (like YOLO), why is Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) performed as a post-processing step?
options: The model predicts multiple overlapping candidate bounding boxes for the same object; NMS keeps the highest-scoring box and deletes overlapping duplicates based on IoU
NMS increases the brightness of detected objects in the final image
NMS converts bounding box coordinates into segmentation masks
It rescales bounding boxes back to the original camera aspect ratio
stage-5.why: Dense detection grids produce many high-confidence boxes around a single detected item. NMS suppresses redundant boxes whose Intersection over Union (IoU) exceeds a threshold.

stage-5.q: Why do standard Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) struggle to maintain dependencies across 200 time steps during backpropagation?
options: Repeated multiplication by the transition weight matrix W_h over 200 steps causes gradients to either vanish to zero or explode to infinity
RNNs erase their memory buffers after every 10 tokens
Hidden states can only store integer values
The chain rule is mathematically invalid for sequential data
stage-5.why: Backpropagation through time involves multiplying the recurrent Jacobian across every time step: W^200. If the spectral radius of W != 1, gradients decay or explode exponentially.

stage-5.q: Why has subword tokenization (such as Byte-Pair Encoding or WordPiece) completely replaced fixed word-level vocabularies in modern language models?
options: It handles arbitrary out-of-vocabulary words and typos gracefully by decomposing rare words into common subword pieces with a compact vocabulary
It converts words directly into 1024-dimensional floating-point vectors without an embedding table
It guarantees that every token corresponds to exactly one syllable
Subword tokenization prevents text from containing punctuation
stage-5.why: Word vocabularies cannot hold every rare word or typo. Character models are too slow. BPE balances both: frequent words get single tokens, while rare words are broken into pieces.

stage-5.q: In word embedding spaces (like Word2Vec), why does the vector arithmetic 'king - man + woman' land remarkably close to the vector for 'queen'?
options: The objective forces direction vectors to encode linear semantic relationships (such as gender and royalty) across co-occurrence contexts
The authors hand-crafted offset values for royal words into the dictionary
Cosine similarity is only defined for words with identical lengths
The dot product of all English nouns is constrained to equal 1
stage-5.why: Predicting context words forces semantic shifts (like male-to-female) to be represented by consistent directional offset vectors in the learned latent space.

stage-5.q: In the self-attention formula Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / √d_k) V, what is the critical role of dividing by √d_k?
options: When dimension d_k is large, dot products grow large, pushing softmax into regions with tiny gradients; √d_k scales variance back to 1
It prevents the matrix multiplication from producing negative numbers
It normalizes the sequence length to match batch size
It converts query vectors into valid probability distributions
stage-5.why: For independent zero-mean unit-variance components, the dot product has variance d_k. Dividing by √d_k restores unit variance, preventing softmax saturation.

stage-5.q: Why must decoder-only autoregressive transformers (like GPT) use a causal attention mask during training?
options: To prevent tokens at position t from attending to future tokens at t+1, ensuring the model only predicts the next word from preceding context
To prevent attention matrices from using more than 50% of GPU memory
To force the model to generate words in reverse alphabetical order
Because GPUs cannot multiply upper-triangular matrices
stage-5.why: During training, all tokens are fed in parallel. If position t could attend to position t+1, it would trivially copy the target answer instead of learning to predict it.

stage-6.q: When building an application with an LLM, when should you prefer few-shot prompt engineering over fine-tuning the model weights?
options: When you have fewer than a few hundred examples, need rapid iteration on instructions, or want to avoid training and hosting specialized model checkpoints
When you need the model to output lower-latency audio waveforms
When your task requires changing the tokenizer vocabulary
When the context window of the model is zero tokens
stage-6.why: In-context few-shot prompting works immediately with zero training costs, no GPU infrastructure, and trivial iteration. Fine-tuning is reserved for style, domain syntax, or token economics at scale.

stage-6.q: In a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, why is hybrid search (combining BM25 keyword search with dense vector embeddings) usually superior to vector search alone?
options: Dense vectors capture high-level semantic meaning, while BM25 catches exact keyword matches (part numbers, error codes, unique names) that dense embeddings often blur
BM25 runs on the client browser while vector search runs in the cloud
Vector search only works on English text, while BM25 works on numbers
Hybrid search eliminates the need for an LLM to generate answers
stage-6.why: Dense embeddings excel at conceptual paraphrasing ('fix leaky pipe'), but fail on exact alphanumeric queries ('Model XR-902A error 404'). Hybrid search captures both.

stage-6.q: How does Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) allow efficient fine-tuning of a 70-billion-parameter LLM on consumer GPUs?
options: It freezes the original pretrained weights W and injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices (A and B where ΔW = B * A, rank r << d), updating under 1% of parameters
It prunes 90% of the network layers before fine-tuning begins
It converts 16-bit floating point numbers into 1-bit integers
It restricts fine-tuning exclusively to the first embedding layer
stage-6.why: LoRA freezes the heavy base model and trains two tiny low-rank matrices per attention projection. This dramatically cuts memory needed for optimizer states and gradients.

stage-6.q: When using an LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate generation quality, what common systematic bias must you guard against by swapping order?
options: Position bias: LLM judges frequently favor whichever candidate response is presented first (or second) in the prompt regardless of quality
Alphabetical bias toward words starting with vowels
Recency bias where the LLM forgets the first sentence of the prompt
Token length bias where the LLM always prefers responses with an even number of words
stage-6.why: LLM judges exhibit marked position bias (often preferring Option A). Evaluating both (A, B) and (B, A) and averaging results is standard practice.

stage-6.q: What is the core loop of an autonomous LLM agent using the ReAct (Reason + Act) framework?
options: Thought (reasoning about the current state) -> Action (invoking a specific tool with arguments) -> Observation (reading the tool's result) -> Repeat until solved
Embedding all input documents -> Computing cosine similarity -> Printing top results
Generating code -> Compiling with gcc -> Rebooting the operating system
Running gradient descent on user prompts before answering
stage-6.why: ReAct combines explicit verbal reasoning with tool execution. The agent plans its step, calls a tool, observes output, and uses that feedback to choose the next action.

stage-6.q: Why does structured output enforcement (such as JSON schema decoding with constrained grammar sampling) drastically reduce agent failures?
options: It masks invalid tokens during sampling so the model cannot produce syntactically malformed JSON or unparseable function arguments
It makes the LLM run 10x faster by bypassing the attention layers
It replaces the need for API keys when calling external tools
It prevents the user from typing prompts longer than 100 characters
stage-6.why: Constrained decoding forces the LLM's next-token logits to zero for any token that would violate the grammar, guaranteeing 100% syntactically valid function calls.

stage-6.q: When comparing two text embeddings that have been L2-normalized (length = 1.0), what is the relationship between their cosine similarity and their dot product?
options: Their dot product is exactly equal to their cosine similarity
The dot product is the square root of the cosine similarity
The cosine similarity is always zero when vectors are normalized
The dot product must be divided by 2π to get cosine similarity
stage-6.why: Cosine similarity is defined as (u · v) / (||u|| ||v||). If ||u|| = 1 and ||v|| = 1, the denominator is 1, making cosine similarity identical to the dot product.

stage-6.q: Why is it dangerous to give an LLM agent write access to shell commands or databases without human confirmation or sandboxing?
options: Prompt injections in untrusted inputs can hijack the agent's reasoning and trick it into running destructive commands (like deleting files or exfiltrating data)
Shell commands consume GPU VRAM that the LLM needs for inference
Database drivers are incompatible with transformer architectures
LLMs cannot parse text output from terminal programs
stage-6.why: If an agent reads untrusted text (emails, web pages) containing malicious prompts, the agent can be coerced into issuing destructive shell or SQL commands unless sandboxed.

stage-7.q: Why do high-throughput ML inference servers (like Triton or vLLM) employ dynamic request batching rather than processing each request one by one?
options: GPUs have thousands of cores that remain underutilized on single requests; batching multiple concurrent requests saturates memory bandwidth and multiplies throughput
Dynamic batching reduces the network bandwidth required by client HTTP requests
Batching eliminates the need to load model weights into GPU VRAM
Processing requests individually causes numerical round-off errors
stage-7.why: Inference on single inputs is memory-bandwidth bound (reading weights for one vector). Batching amortizes weight-loading across multiple queries, dramatically boosting throughput.

stage-7.q: Why is exporting a PyTorch model to ONNX or TensorRT preferred over saving and loading a raw Python pickle file in production?
options: ONNX provides an optimized, platform-independent computational graph without Python runtime overhead or arbitrary code-execution security vulnerabilities
Python pickle files cannot store floating-point numbers
TensorRT models can only be trained with unsupervised learning
ONNX files automatically retrain themselves when data changes
stage-7.why: Pickles require a Python runtime and can execute malicious code on unpickling. ONNX/TensorRT provides a standalone graph engine with fused kernels, lower latency, and safety.

stage-7.q: What is the difference between covariate shift and concept drift in a deployed production model?
options: Covariate shift means the distribution of input features P(X) changes, while concept drift means the true relationship between inputs and targets P(Y|X) changes
Covariate shift occurs only on weekends, while concept drift occurs only on weekdays
Covariate shift affects classification models, while concept drift affects regression models
Covariate shift is solved by increasing learning rate, while concept drift requires decreasing it
stage-7.why: If camera lighting changes, P(X) shifted (covariate shift). If economic inflation changes how income relates to default, the underlying relationship P(Y|X) shifted (concept drift).

stage-7.q: What is a 'shadow deployment' (dark launch) of a newly trained machine learning model?
options: Incoming production traffic is mirrored to the new model in parallel with the current model, recording predictions and latencies without serving them to real users
The model is deployed exclusively between midnight and 6 am
The model weights are encrypted so developers cannot inspect them
The model only receives synthetic mock data generated by unit tests
stage-7.why: Shadowing tests the new model's latency, stability, resource utilization, and predictions against live traffic with zero risk to customer experience.

stage-7.q: When training a model to predict elevator breakdowns from IoT telemetry, why must feature joins be performed as 'point-in-time' (as-of) joins?
options: To ensure each feature value reflects strictly what was known at the exact prediction timestamp, preventing lookahead leakage from future maintenance logs
Because time-series databases cannot store timestamps older than 30 days
Point-in-time joins convert non-stationary series into Gaussian distributions
To reduce the number of rows in the training table by half
stage-7.why: Joining with future state (e.g., using a repair record created 2 hours after the outage) leaks the outcome into the features, causing models to fail in live deployment.

stage-7.q: Why is runtime data validation (e.g. checking null counts, types, and schema ranges on inference inputs) essential before passing data to an ML model?
options: Models will quietly output confident, nonsensical predictions when fed out-of-range or missing numbers, rather than throwing clean errors
Passing raw floats causes GPU hardware to overheat
Validation converts non-linear models into linear classifiers
Inference servers refuse HTTP requests that don't include unit tests
stage-7.why: Unlike standard software that crashes on bad input, ML models silently calculate mathematically valid but completely wrong predictions on corrupted data.

stage-7.q: In an elevator failure prediction problem where only 0.2% of elevator-hours experience an outage, why is 99.8% accuracy a useless baseline metric?
options: A trivial model that always predicts 'no breakdown' achieves 99.8% accuracy while catching exactly 0 breakdowns, rendering it worthless for operations
Accuracy cannot be calculated when class percentages are decimals
99.8% accuracy causes false positives to become negative numbers
Elevators cannot be monitored using binary classification
stage-7.why: Under severe class imbalance, majority-class guessing achieves high accuracy while completely failing the real operational objective (finding failures).

stage-7.q: If your live inference microservice experiences a network timeout connecting to the GPU cluster, what constitutes a reliable graceful degradation strategy?
options: Fallback to a cached prediction, a lightweight heuristic model, or a safe default rule so the client application does not crash
Immediately retry the request 1,000 times in a tight while-loop
Return a 500 Internal Server Error and terminate the client session
Delete the model checkpoint from disk and re-trigger training
stage-7.why: Production architectures use fallbacks (heuristics, cached responses, conservative defaults) to preserve user uptime when heavy ML models encounter transient failures.
